evals.prompt: Our Bedrock agent in us-east-1 is returning empty responses in production, but when we test it in the console it works. We prepared a new version yesterday. The agent is in an account that isn't connected here. What I can tell you: the app calls alias 'prod', GetAgentAlias shows prod routing to version 3, version 3 has a guardrail attached, the DRAFT has no guardrail, and tracing is off. What should we check, and what is the likely cause?
evals.expected_output: A review of the Bedrock Agent (LLM-AGT family) that uses the alias-to-version mapping given (prod serves version 3, not the newly prepared DRAFT) before concluding anything about production, rather than assuming the latest prepared DRAFT is live. It checks whether a guardrail is attached (LLM-AGT-001) because an intervening guardrail can present as empty output, whether the application is pinned to a stable published-version alias rather than the test alias / DRAFT (LLM-AGT-007), and whether tracing is enabled so the orchestration can be inspected (LLM-AGT-005). Each finding carries a catalog check-id and a severity, no raw account id is exposed, and no agent session content or prompt-override text is reproduced.
assertions: The response resolves the agent alias to its served version before concluding what production runs, rather than treating the latest prepared DRAFT as live

The response checks whether a guardrail is attached to the agent as a possible cause of empty output, and routes guardrail policy-strength questions elsewhere rather than evaluating the policy content here
The response names an ordered set of concrete checks (alias resolution, guardrail attachment, tracing) rather than generic 'check your agent' advice
Each finding carries a severity and the concrete observed signal that triggered it, not an unsupported assertion

assertions.text: At least one finding carries an AGT or AC catalog check-id
No raw 12-digit account ID is exposed

evals.prompt: Our Bedrock AgentCore runtime llmops_eval_billing_agent in us-east-1 can't invoke its model and every request errors. Check this account and tell me here in chat what's wrong.
evals.expected_output: An AgentCore (LLM-AC family) review that reads the runtime (GetAgentRuntime) for its execution role and the model it calls, evaluates the execution role's policies for bedrock:InvokeModel on that model, and finds the action is not allowed, raising LLM-AC-001 with its severity. It considers an SCP explicit deny (LLM-AC-002) or says it could not read SCPs from this account. It gives the missing policy statement as a change for the operator to make, does not apply it, does not blame a Bedrock service event, and masks the account segment of any ARN it shows.
assertions: The response inspects the runtime's execution role for the model-invoke permission rather than guessing at the cause
The response identifies the missing bedrock:InvokeModel permission on the execution role as the cause
The response gives the policy fix as a change for the operator to make and does not claim to have applied it

assertions.text: No raw 12-digit account ID is exposed

evals.prompt: Our AgentCore runtime cost_estimator_agent_with_identity in us-east-1 rejects every request from our web app with an unauthorized error. The JWT comes from our Cognito user pool and decodes fine: iss is the pool's issuer URL, token_use is access, client_id is web-app-spa, and it has no aud claim. Check this account and tell me here in chat what is wrong.
evals.expected_output: Reads the runtime's inbound authorizer (GetAgentRuntime authorizerConfiguration.customJWTAuthorizer): a Cognito discovery URL and an allowedClients list with one entry, and no allowedAudience. Compares it with the claims given and concludes that the token's client_id (web-app-spa) is not the allowed client, so the authorizer rejects a token that is otherwise valid. Says this is a configuration mismatch, not an expired or malformed token, and gives the fix as a step for the operator: add the web app's client ID to allowedClients, or have the web app request tokens for the allowed client. Applies nothing itself and masks any account ID.
assertions: The response reads the runtime's inbound JWT authorizer configuration rather than guessing
The response identifies the client ID mismatch (the token's client_id is not in allowedClients) as the cause
The response distinguishes a configuration mismatch from an expired, malformed or wrongly signed token
The response gives the fix as a step for the operator and does not claim to have changed the authorizer

assertions.text: No raw 12-digit account ID is exposed

evals.prompt: Adding a new tool to our AgentCore gateway target makes the whole target fail to load, and the other tools disappear too. Why does one tool break all of them?
evals.expected_output: The answer explains that tool definitions are validated as a set, so one invalid schema can fail the whole target load, and identifies the kind of schema defect responsible (duplicate names or operation ids, unsupported types, missing required fields). It tells the user how to find the offending definition.
assertions: The response explains why one bad tool definition can fail the entire target rather than being skipped
The response names a specific class of schema defect to look for
The response gives a concrete way to isolate the offending tool

assertions.text: No raw 12-digit account ID is exposed

evals.prompt: Our AgentCore deployment fails with: 'User: arn:aws:sts::<account>:assumed-role/agentcore-deployer/ci is not authorized to perform: bedrock-agentcore:CreateAgentRuntime with an explicit deny'. The deployer role's identity policy allows bedrock-agentcore:*. It runs in an account that isn't connected here, so answer from what I've told you: where can the deny come from, and how do we find which one it is?
evals.expected_output: The answer identifies an explicit deny that overrides the role's allow, most commonly a service control policy, a permissions boundary, or a VPC endpoint policy, and explains that an explicit deny always wins over an allow. It says how to determine which one applies.
assertions: The response identifies an explicit deny source such as an SCP, permissions boundary, or endpoint policy
The response explains that an explicit deny overrides an allow in the role policy
The response gives a concrete way to identify which policy is responsible

assertions.text: No raw 12-digit account ID is exposed

evals.prompt: We cannot see end-to-end traces for our AgentCore agent, only isolated log lines. What we see: `aws xray get-trace-segment-destination` returns XRay (not CloudWatchLogs), and the agent's container has no OTEL_* environment variables and does not start through opentelemetry-instrument. What is wrong, and how do we get a connected view of a request?
evals.expected_output: Uses the state given: CloudWatch Transaction Search is off (the trace segment destination is XRay, not CloudWatchLogs) and the agent is not instrumented with OpenTelemetry, so spans are neither emitted nor indexed, and isolated log lines cannot be joined into one request. Names both prerequisites, explains why each is needed, and gives the fixes as steps for the operator: enable Transaction Search (update-trace-segment-destination to CloudWatchLogs with the logs resource policy) and instrument the agent (ADOT / opentelemetry-instrument with trace-context propagation). Applies nothing itself.
assertions: The response concludes from the destination given that CloudWatch Transaction Search is not enabled
The response identifies the missing OpenTelemetry instrumentation as the second cause
The response explains why isolated log lines cannot be correlated without these
The response gives the fixes as steps for the operator and does not claim to have changed anything

assertions.text: No raw 12-digit account ID is exposed

evals.prompt: Our AgentCore agent forgets context between turns even though we configured memory. What should we check?
evals.expected_output: The answer checks that memory is both configured and actually referenced on the invocation path: the memory resource's state, the identifier the agent passes, the session or actor key used to scope retrieval, and the role's permission to read and write it. It names the most likely break rather than restating the feature.
assertions: The response checks that the agent actually passes the memory and session or actor identifier on invocation
The response considers permissions to read and write memory
The response distinguishes memory not being written from memory not being retrieved

assertions.text: No raw 12-digit account ID is exposed
